video_title: The US Can Stop China's Import Loophole | Nick Brown
gist: Nick Brown (Center for Technology and Statecraft) argues that DUV immersion lithography, chiefly ASML's NXT 1980 still sold to China (~90 systems, $10B+ in 2024-25), is the decisive chokepoint: cutting imports locks in a US AI-chip lead through 2035, while continued flows could allow near-parity in a decade. The episode dissects the MATCH Act (countrywide allied SME controls, servicing, 150-day negotiation), a US-Japan light-source workaround, allied political economy and Beijing's likely muted retaliation.

insights.claim: Median estimates as of October 2026 put China at roughly 1 million H100-equivalents of compute versus upwards of 30 million for the US, though all such numbers are hazy.
insights.speaker: Akib (ChinaTalk co-host)
insights.so_what: Baseline for sizing the US compute lead that export-control policy is trying to preserve.
insights.quote: you could say that China currently has maybe around a million. Uh whereas the US has upwards of 30 million

insights.claim: China can additionally reach close to another million H100-equivalents via remote access to data centers in Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia), so the worst-case US compute advantage is about 10x rather than 30x.
insights.speaker: Akib (ChinaTalk co-host)
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian data-center capacity is a material leak in US compute controls; watch remote-access/cloud KYC rules.

insights.claim: Of compute, algorithms and data, compute is the most governable AI input, making it the natural policy lever for shaping China's AI capability.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Explains why chip and tool export controls remain the central US AI-competition policy instrument.

insights.claim: US leverage differs by chip category: remotely accessed chips can be cut off at any moment, exported chips give leverage only at the point of export, and indigenously produced Chinese chips offer very little leverage at all.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Policy that limits China's indigenous chipmaking capacity matters more long-term than debates over how many Nvidia chips to export.

insights.claim: If China can make as many chips as it wants with its own supply chain, the compute chokepoint ceases to be an effective tool for shaping international power.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Indigenous capacity, not export volume of H20/H200-class chips, is the key variable for long-run US advantage.

insights.claim: The right way to judge US-China compute competition is relative chipmaking advantage (ratios) and absolute capability thresholds, not a binary 'beat China or not' frame; there is no magic number for a comfortable lead.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Analysts should track production ratios over time rather than headline parity moments.

themes.theme: DUV lithography as China's binding chokepoint

insights.claim: Advanced DUV immersion machines sell for $60-80 million versus hundreds of millions for EUV, yet the most advanced DUV tools are capable of manufacturing China's flagship Huawei Ascend AI chips.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: The EUV ban alone does not stop Chinese AI chip production; DUV access is the live policy question.

insights.claim: Lithography is the hardest semiconductor tool for China to indigenize and will be the last one it masters; China has 0% market share in lithography while making inroads in etch, deposition and CMP.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Litho is the most durable export-control chokepoint; Chinese etch/deposition makers are more likely to gain share domestically.

insights.claim: ASML's NXT 1980 DUV immersion system, which the US and allies still allow into China, is good enough for the 7nm logic and HBM2E (maybe some HBM3) used in Huawei's current AI chips.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: ASML's China immersion sales directly feed Huawei AI accelerator capacity and are exposed to tighter controls.
insights.quote: we have a big um big cannonball sized hole. It's not really a loophole hole. We'd call it a cannonball hole um in our export controls

insights.claim: China imported about 90 DUV immersion systems in 2024 and 2025, worth over $10 billion and close to two-thirds of ASML's entire DUV immersion exports.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: ASML's immersion revenue is heavily China-concentrated, so a countrywide control would hit a large share of that product line.

insights.claim: China already has an estimated 340 ASML lithography systems in-country, split between advanced and legacy fabs, which Nick Brown calls a strategic loss for the US.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: The installed base sets China's existing litho-bounded chip ceiling regardless of future controls.

insights.claim: A single ASML NXT 1980 system can likely produce over 100,000 Huawei Ascend chips per year, even assuming China's much worse yields.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Each marginal immersion scanner shipped to China translates into large AI chip capacity, so even small import volumes matter.

insights.claim: China's 2024-2025 DUV 'stockpile' is not sitting in warehouses but installed and in active use in fabs, meaning that capacity can be redirected toward AI chips.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Installed capacity in smartphone/other production is latent AI chip capacity that could be reallocated quickly.

insights.claim: Even under a hyper-aggressive scenario where China prototypes an NXT 1980-equivalent next year, reaches commercial production the year after, and scales 100% year-over-year, its existing stockpile plus indigenous output does not come close to US-allied production if imports are cut off.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Cutting DUV imports is seen as locking in a durable US chipmaking lead regardless of Chinese litho indigenization claims.
insights.quote: It is a button that lets you win the AI competition at least as measured by uh chipm.

insights.claim: China will not indigenize DUV lithography at a scale sufficient to substantially expand its chipmaking until into the 2030s; prototype, commercial qualification and scale-up are separate serial hurdles, and 5-20 domestic systems would not move the needle.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Discount near-term Chinese announcements of domestic lithography prototypes; scaled output is what matters.

insights.claim: Nobody can match ASML in lithography, which is precisely why lithography offers so much export-control leverage.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: ASML's monopoly position cuts both ways: pricing power and geopolitical exposure to US pressure.

insights.claim: China's current lithography stockpile is physically incapable of matching US AI chip production through 2035; even devoting 100% of tools to AI chips would yield well below about a tenth of US production.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: With imports halted, the US compute lead is structurally guaranteed for a decade.

insights.claim: If China keeps importing lithography at the 2024-2025 rate and makes a concerted 'AI push' allocation, Chinese AI chip production could approach near-parity with the US within about 10 years.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Continued DUV flows convert a guaranteed US advantage into real uncertainty about the compute balance.

insights.claim: Chinese litho-bounded AI chip capacity is driven by three variables: the pace of tool imports, the share of tools sitting in AI-capable fabs like SMIC and CXMT, and the share of those fabs' output allocated to AI versus phones.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Watch SMIC/CXMT capex and product-mix shifts toward AI accelerators/HBM as leading indicators.

insights.claim: China's DUV import pace could modestly increase into the 2030s as AI grows in importance, even though the 2024-2025 pace was partly driven by stockpiling ahead of controls.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Do not assume Chinese litho demand normalizes downward absent new controls.

insights.claim: In the next one to two years China's chip output is primarily limited by deposition and etch, but over 3-15 years it is untenable to assume China fails to indigenize those tools, making lithography the binding long-run constraint.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Near-term deposition/etch controls buy time; litho controls determine the long-run ceiling.

insights.claim: US chip production into the 2030s may itself become partially limited by EUV tool supply.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: EUV supply could be a constraint on US-allied AI chip output, supporting demand for ASML EUV.

insights.claim: The MATCH Act is a bipartisan, bicameral semiconductor-manufacturing-equipment export bill now in the Senate version of the NDAA, to be fought over in NDAA conference over the next couple of months.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: NDAA conference outcome is the key catalyst for ASML/Tokyo Electron China exposure.

insights.claim: The MATCH Act would elevate DUV immersion and a few other top-tier tools from entity-specific to countrywide China controls, and align allied entity controls on SMIC and CXMT, where the US bans all equipment but Japan and the Netherlands control a much smaller set.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Japanese and Dutch toolmakers' sales to SMIC/CXMT would face the same restrictions US vendors already face.

insights.claim: The MATCH Act directs Commerce/BIS to negotiate with allies for roughly 150 days and, if talks fail, to impose controls unilaterally using existing legal mechanisms; it covers only immersion DUV, not all DUV.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Dry DUV and older tools stay outside scope; the 150-day clock and possible extensions set timing.

insights.claim: The 150-day negotiating window will likely let China stockpile tens to possibly over a hundred more DUV systems before the MATCH Act bites, but that does not fundamentally degrade its decade-long strategic impact.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Expect a pull-forward of Chinese immersion scanner orders before any effective date.
insights.quote: there's nothing that uh government likes to do more than continue negotiations

insights.claim: Cutting off new tool exports is the most impactful part of the MATCH Act; servicing controls could sensibly distinguish advanced fabs (16/14nm logic and below, ~18nm half-pitch memory) from legacy fabs, which would preserve much of toolmakers' service revenue.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: How servicing is written in conference determines the revenue hit to ASML and Tokyo Electron China service businesses.

insights.claim: Ending allied servicing at Chinese advanced fabs would likely not stop production but would degrade yield and throughput starting in about 6-12 months, especially for subsystems like light sources, stages and sensors.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Servicing restrictions are the faster-acting lever versus import bans, which bite over 3-10 years.

insights.claim: China has already imported enough lithography capacity to cover all its smartphone chip demand for the next 10 years, so DUV cutoffs mainly constrain massive AI chipmaking rather than consumer devices.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Collateral damage to Chinese consumer electronics from MATCH is likely small.

insights.claim: The US already unilaterally imposed countrywide controls on about 11 deposition tools in October 2022, mostly from Applied Materials, and many US tools comparable to the NXT 1980 are controlled countrywide, so MATCH is genuinely an alignment action.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: US toolmakers have borne a competitive cost the allies avoided; MATCH would level that field.

insights.claim: The US has handcuffed its own deposition and etching companies expecting Japan to follow suit, and Japan has not, though China seems more able to indigenize deposition and etch so controls there choke less than lithography.
insights.speaker: Akib (ChinaTalk co-host)
insights.so_what: Japanese etch/dep vendors have been winning China share US firms cannot access.
insights.quote: we have deposition and etching companies and we've handcuffed our own with the expectation that Japan was going to follow suit and they haven't

insights.claim: The US and Japan alone could control all DUV immersion exports to China without FDPR or extraterritorial authority, because every immersion system needs a light source from either Cymer (US, ASML-owned) or Gigaphoton (Japan).
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Light-source suppliers are a little-discussed chokepoint that bypasses Dutch reluctance.
insights.quote: the US and Japan can jointly have the effect of controlling all immersion systems to China

insights.claim: The MATCH Act is broadly positive for US and allied chipmakers such as Samsung, SK Hynix, Nvidia, AMD and Intel, because Chinese DUV-enabled chips from Huawei and CXMT would otherwise flood global markets and erode their margins.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Memory makers in particular benefit from capping CXMT's advanced capacity.

insights.claim: Japan is far less exposed than the Netherlands on DUV immersion since Nikon has only a small sliver, and Japanese chipmakers could benefit, though Japan's position is not certain.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Japan may be the easier ally to win over; the Netherlands/ASML bears most of the cost.

insights.claim: Retaliation risk is meaningfully lower for an act of Congress than for executive export controls, because law cannot be undone with a signature and is less likely to get bargained away in trade negotiations.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Legislated controls are more durable and less likely to be traded away in Trump-Xi talks.

insights.claim: Because DUV import bans bite gradually over years rather than overnight, China is less likely to retaliate sharply than it did against 2025's acute measures.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Lower probability of rare-earth-style retaliation tied to MATCH passage.

insights.claim: Jordan Schneider puts a pretty high probability on MATCH not triggering a 'trade war 3.0', since 2025's escalations followed acute shocks like 100-200% tariffs and the 50% rule cutting 10,000+ Chinese firms off from technology, whereas MATCH is a slow burn.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider (host)
insights.so_what: Market risk from MATCH passage is lower than from tariff or entity-list shocks.

insights.claim: The strongest argument against MATCH is that it could replay summer 2025, when China played the rare earths card, factories shut, and the Trump administration found a way to cave.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider (host)
insights.so_what: Rare-earth supply is the key tail risk to watch if MATCH passes.

insights.claim: Beijing is likely to respond to DUV cutoffs as it did to Nvidia chip restrictions, framing it as a push to indigenize rather than throwing down the gauntlet.
insights.speaker: Jordan Schneider (host)
insights.so_what: Expect renewed Chinese domestic litho subsidies and headlines rather than immediate retaliation.

insights.claim: Nick Brown ranks DUV controls as his top compute-policy priority on mid- to long-term horizons, above remote access, because indigenous chipmaking underpins any strategic advantage.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Long-horizon policy focus will stay on SME controls even as chip-export debates dominate headlines.
insights.quote: the foundation of that advantage is indigenous chipm and the foundation of that is lithography

insights.claim: Akib argues compute policy is roughly 90% of the way there and that remote access has the most remaining juice, alongside issues like distillation and RL environments.
insights.speaker: Akib (ChinaTalk co-host)
insights.so_what: Signals live policy debate over whether cloud access rather than tools is the next control frontier.

insights.claim: DUV import-ban impacts materialize over 3-10 years while servicing impacts come within 1-3 years, so under very short AGI timelines the import ban matters less to the strategic outcome.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Your AGI-timeline view determines how much weight to put on SME controls versus faster levers.

insights.claim: A durable US compute lead gives breathing room to decide domestically how a dual-use, society-changing technology should be governed without a rival great power breathing down its neck.
insights.speaker: Nick Brown
insights.so_what: Frames compute advantage as buying governance time, not only military edge.
